{"id": "2:61/q03", "question": "Why did the Israelites ask for other food?", "turns_on": "Former habits, monotony, desire for settlement, social dependence, or appetite and ingratitude.", "positions": [{"id": "2:61/q03/p1", "position": "They wanted other produce", "reasons": "AKHFASH: Alternatively, من can be treated as extra, as in “I saw no one” or “did a man come to you?” TAB-FULL: Kufr is covering or concealing; God’s signs are His proofs, evidences, and indications of His oneness and His messengers’ truthfulness. TAB-FULL: The charge means they denied God’s proofs of His oneness and the messengers’ truth, rejected their force, and called them lies. WAHIDI-BASIT (الفرزدق): His line to Muʿāwiya uses بؤت to mean ‘I would have acknowledged it,’ as if taking the place of one who confesses it. JISHUMI: Wāḥid can mean one, the first number, or what cannot be divided; God is one through uniqueness in His praiseworthy attributes. KASHSHAF-FULL: The requested greens are choice vegetables eaten by people, such as mint, celery and leek. TABRISI (الفرزدق): Al-Farazdaq's image of a spider's web spread over someone illustrates the idiom of something being laid upon them. TABRISI: Anger means the will to inflict harm; when attributed to God it means His will to punish the one under wrath. TABRISI: Wāḥid is the first number; God is one because He is distinguished by His most beautiful attributes. RAZI-FULL: Abu Muslim's side answers that ownership normally entails unrestricted use, and barring entry contradicts that default without evidence. QURTUBI-FULL: Asking someone to feed one a report means asking them to tell it; an imam's being asked to be fed means prompting him when he loses his recitation. QURTUBI-FULL: Second, God's gift came with a command to eat it, so continuing in obedience and gratitude brought afterlife reward, unlike their request. NASAFI-FULL: The requested greens are the earth's vegetables, especially choice herbs such as mint, celery and leek. ABUHAYYAN-FULL: Wāḥid means indivisible or something to which no second is added; waḥada/yahidu means to be alone. ABUHAYYAN-FULL: The pronoun could instead refer to God, supported by the ensuing command and promise. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (أبي): Ubayy reads أتبدلون; the wording is figurative because God alone effects the change, but their request makes them seem to change it. ABUHAYYAN-FULL: A commentator mistakenly split Zuhayr al-Kisa'i into two people when attributing the anomalous reading; Zuhayr al-Kisa'i and al-Farqabi are one man. ABUHAYYAN-FULL: The verb باء is used with good outcomes as well as evil ones, contrary to the claim that it occurs only for evil. ABUHAYYAN-FULL: The definite wording can instead emphasize totality: no right existed, whether recognized by Muslims or anyone else. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (الخليل بن أحمد): Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad subsisted on barley flour and fresh water, yet had an exceptionally bright mind and strong body, campaigning one year and making pilgrimage the next. SAMIN-DURR (أبو البقاء): Abu al-Baqa regards the indefinite-relative analysis as weak because the request refers to a specific thing, not an unspecified one. BIQAI-FULL (الحرالي): Al-Harali says cities rarely exhibit extraordinary breaks in ordinary order; ascetics therefore seek travel and withdrawal from inhabited places to experience provision by God's word without the burden of His established order. BURSEVI: The clause beginning “He said” is a new sentence answering an implied question about what God or Moses replied. ALUSI-FULL: Calling the requested items simply ما avoids naming them directly as a sign of disdain. ALUSI-FULL (قيل): One reply distinguishes the prophets who were killed from the messengers promised help. ALUSI-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbas is reported to say that God decreed that seventy thousand people would be killed for each prophet and thirty-five thousand for each caliph; the author finds this answer unsound. IBNASHUR-FULL: The بدل family means putting one thing or quality in place of another, or compensating one thing with another. IBNASHUR-FULL (أبو الطيب): Abū al-Ṭayyib’s couplet offers a parallel reproach: if this year pleases you, return to Homs next year."}, {"id": "2:61/q03/p2", "position": "Weariness and desire for variety", "reasons": "TAB-FULL (قتادة): Qatada says they tired of their food and recalled the way of life they had before, which prompted their request for produce. IBNABIHATIM (قتادة): Qatada says they tired of their food and recalled the life they had before. WAHIDI-BASIT (سعيد بن المسيب): Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib says the people had grown tired of their way of life. BAGHAWI-FULL: The Israelites grew weary of eating manna and quail. KASHSHAF-FULL: The people had been farmers; returning to their old habits made them weary of their blessing and desirous of misery. TABRISI (قتادة): Qatada says the people were shaded by clouds and given manna and quails in the wilderness, tired of them, recalled life in Egypt, and asked Moses for its produce. DURR-FULL (قتادة): Qatada says they had tired of their wilderness food and recalled the life they had before, prompting their request to Moses. BURSEVI: In the wilderness they tired of unchanging manna and quail, remembered their former agricultural life in Egypt, and longed for familiar habits."}, {"id": "2:61/q03/p3", "position": "Longing for former food and habits", "reasons": "TAB-FULL (قتادة): Qatada says they tired of their food and recalled the way of life they had before, which prompted their request for produce. TAB-FULL (قتادة): In another report, Qatada says that after reaching Syria they lacked their former foods and asked Moses for crops. IBNABIHATIM (قتادة): Qatada says they tired of their food and recalled the life they had before. THALABI (الحسن): The Israelites were people accustomed to leeks, onions, and lentils; they reverted to their bad former habits and craved familiar foods, so they rejected manna and quails. KASHSHAF-FULL: The people had been farmers; returning to their old habits made them weary of their blessing and desirous of misery. {"id": "2:61/q04", "question": "What does their claim that they cannot endure mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:61/q04/p1", "position": "Restraint or endurance of the self", "reasons": "TAB-FULL (ابن زيد): Ibn Zayd says the command means a town; he takes it to be the holy land God assigned to Israel, citing 5:21. JISHUMI: Ṣabr is restraint of the self from what it desires, opposite to panic; the cited poem contrasts patience with panic. JISHUMI (الحسن وأبو العالية والربيع والأعمش): Another view identifies the destination as Pharaoh’s Egypt; another identifies it as Jerusalem, where they could obtain the plants they wanted. JISHUMI (قيل): Another explanation says they had grown tired of the wilderness and were too ashamed to state that plainly, so they hinted at it indirectly. BAGHAWI-FULL: The familiar reading omits the hamza; one explanation is that it was dropped for ease because the word is used frequently. IBNATIYYA-FULL (الأخفش): Al-Akhfash permits inflecting the name because of its lightness and resemblance to Hind and Daʿd; Sibawayh does not permit this. IBNATIYYA-FULL (غير الأخفش): Another explanation says the word is inflected because it denotes a place. TABRISI: Another explanation says they sought produce so the poor could assist the rich, rather than having everyone equally rich and independent. IBNJAWZI-ZAD: Baqalat and abqalat are both eloquent forms for land sprouting vegetation; ibtaqalat describes camels grazing. RAZI-FULL: Their request may have been driven by weariness with the wilderness and a desire to reach settled lands, rather than by the foods themselves. RAZI-FULL: An objection says the command to enter the Holy Land may be recommendatory and therefore need not bar entry into Egypt; Razi invokes the principle that an imperative is presumptively obligatory. RAZI-FULL: Even if entering the Holy Land were only recommended, allowing the prophets to abandon a recommended duty would be improper. RAZI-FULL: A reply says do not turn back can mean do not disobey the command or deny the Holy Land's superiority, or the prohibition may apply only for a specified time; Razi finds that limitation contrary to the apparent sense. RAZI-FULL: Razi says the context makes do not turn back refer to the immediately preceding order to enter the Holy Land, while restricting the prohibition to a particular time departs from its apparent meaning. RAZI-FULL: An objection says owning a house does not always permit entry, as when a person observing mosque retreat owns a home; perhaps Israel's inheritance meant authority while the Holy Land command barred entry. QURTUBI-FULL (عكرمة عن ابن عباس): ʿIkrimah transmits Ibn ʿAbbās's explanation: a town among these towns. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (قيل): The tanwin may still indicate an unspecified city, specifically one among the cities of the Holy Land, as supported by the command to enter the Holy Land. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (قيل): Another explanation treats the phrase as emphatic because no prophet ever brought anything warranting death; those killed were hated, and their killing raised their rank. ABUHAYYAN-FULL: One explanation takes definite الحق as an allusion to the established rule in the Prophetic hadith that Muslim blood is protected except in three cases. SAMIN-DURR: On the near-in-this-world interpretation, the superior food's benefit is obtained in the afterlife through patience. SAMIN-DURR: Alternatively it may be an accusative circumstantial phrase describing the omitted pronoun returning to ما; من remains explanatory. SAMIN-DURR: The Prophet's ban on saying راعنا is analogous: the Jews could exploit that word as an insult in their language; alternatively, it encouraged choosing the most eloquent language. BIQAI-FULL: لن نصبر means they would not endure the food for long. BURSEVI (قيل): An alternative explanation is that they could not bear everyone being self-sufficient, since mutual aid would disappear; they were also early adopters of servants and slaves. BURSEVI: This community would not have spoken like Israel because of its brighter lights and penetrating spiritual insight; it is the balanced community of 2:143. ALUSI-FULL (قيل): Another explanation confines the prohibition to early Islam, when Jewish subterfuge was prevalent, as with replacing راعنا by انظرنا. IBNASHUR-FULL: The episode shifts from favors to Israel's poor choice of appetite, which may still be lawful, but their words show discourtesy toward Moses and the benefactor: ‘we cannot endure’ casts the given food as hateful."}]}
{"id": "2:61/q05", "question": "Was their request sinful?", "turns_on": "Whether the request rejects God's choice, and whether rebuke or a grant establishes sin.", "positions": [{"id": "2:61/q05/p1", "position": "Sinful ingratitude", "reasons": "IBNABIHATIM (الحسن): Al-Hasan says they were ungrateful, recalled their former life, and requested the vegetables and foods they used to eat. WAHIDI-BASIT: They called it one food because manna with quail was eaten together like one dish and presented as one color, although made from different ingredients. JISHUMI: Some say the request was not sinful because both foods were permitted; others say it was sinful because they resented God’s choice, which the author regards as stronger. TABRISI: The more apt view is that the request was sinful because they were reproached for refusing what God chose. RAZI-FULL (الظاهريون من المفسرين): Most literalist commentators hold that the request for another kind of food was sinful, but Razi rejects this view. Against — RAZI-FULL: Razi argues that manna and quail had been permitted rather than commanded, so asking for another food was permissible, including asking through Moses because that seemed likelier to be answered. Against — RAZI-FULL: Razi says the rhetorical rebuke may concern losing a greater worldly benefit or a greater afterlife benefit, rather than sin in the request itself. RAZI-FULL: An objection reads their inability to endure one food as proof they disliked the manna and quail, making the request sinful. Against — RAZI-FULL: Razi replies that they expressed desire for another food, not dissatisfaction with what they had; the future negation in lan does not establish resentment toward the present food. RAZI-FULL: A counterargument says guaranteed food disliked by their tastes was harder to consume than desired food obtained with effort; Razi answers that certain present benefit still outweighs uncertain distant benefit. Against — ABUHAYYAN-FULL: Abū Ḥayyān replies that saying they could not endure one food shows a desire for other foods, not necessarily dissatisfaction with what God provided; a rebuke may concern forfeiting worldly or afterlife benefit. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (قيل): Another interpretation says they meant they could not endure everyone being wealthy and no one needing to serve another; the one food represents their common status in the wilderness before social differences returned. ABUHAYYAN-FULL: Because replacing one food kind with another is a reasonable aim and the Qurʾān does not say they were forbidden to ask, the request cannot be treated as sinful. IBNKATHIR-FULL (الحسن البصري): Al-Hasan says they showed ingratitude, would not endure the provision, and recalled the diet they had lived on before. ALUSI-FULL: The author endorses al-Salikuti's judgment that al-Razi's inference is weak: granting the request does not make their ungrateful demand virtuous. ALUSI-FULL: Although inability to endure one food might imply wanting an addition, their aversion and ingratitude imply a wish to remove the blessing and replace it. ELMALILI: Monotony may bore human desire, but seeking variety is not itself sinful. IBNASHUR-FULL: This sentence continues the preceding pattern of recounting God's favors, whether pure favors or favors mixed with ingratitude and subsequent pardon, so its content should also be a favor. IBNASHUR-FULL: A reading transmitted through al-Fakhr and explained by ʿAbd al-Ḥakīm says asking to replace manna and quail was sinful ingratitude: ‘patience’ implies dislike, and the rebuke confirms it; the favor was pardon and the concession to go down. IBNASHUR-FULL: God's answer withdraws special care: instead of providing food, water, and shade as before, He orders them to go to a town and procure their own, a disciplinary rebuke for their attitude rather than punishment for a sinful request. IBNASHUR-FULL: Worldly deprivation and loss of spiritual gifts are not consequences of a legal sin under divine command; they resemble causal ordering in the world's system. Only afterlife punishment proves the act was sinful, resolving the interpretive difficulty. IBNASHUR-FULL: The jussive يخرج replaces an expected أن يخرج, presenting the result as certain if Moses asks and pressing him to act for their benefit. IBNASHUR-FULL: The واء rather than فاء makes the punishment an independently asserted report of what their ingratitude merited, not merely a consequence attached to Moses’s rebuke."}, {"id": "2:61/q05/p2", "position": "The rebuke ce

{"id": "2:61/q06", "question": "How is the final rāʾ of نَّصْبِرَ treated at pause?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:61/q06/p1", "position": "Pause treatment depends on rāʾ and preceding sound", "reasons": "NASHR: A final rāʾ that is open, including نصبر, is stopped on with sukūn only; the author sets out parallel categories for still, transferred-kasra and other final rāʾs. NASHR: When final rāʾ has a permanent lexical or inflectional kasra, pause permits rawm or sukūn; a nominative ending permits rawm, ishāmām, or sukūn. NASHR: At pause with sukūn or ishāmām, tarqīq is the established rule when the preceding sound is kasra, sukūn after kasra, silent yāʾ, imāla, or a soft rāʾ; otherwise the rāʾ is tafkhīm. NASHR: Some soften a rāʾ with its own kasra at pause on the ground that pause makes the preceding state temporary; the author notes a possible distinction between temporary and permanent kasra. NASHR: With rawm, a kasra softens rāʾ for all; a ḍamma is softened only by Warsh through al-Azraq after specified triggers, while other cases are tafkhīm, with some distinction for a kasra ending."}]}
{"id": "2:61/q07", "question": "What was the 'one food,' and why was it called one?", "turns_on": "Whether one describes a repeated regimen, mixed meal, food class, single item, or shared prosperity.", "positions": [{"id": "2:61/q07/p1", "position": "Manna and quail together", "reasons": "TAB-FULL (ابن أبي نجيح): Ibn Abi Najih says their one food was manna and quail, which they sought to replace with vegetables and the other listed crops. IBNABIHATIM (أبو العالية): The Israelites had quails for food and manna for drink, and said they could not endure that single fare. THALABI: Although manna and quail are two foods, the Arabs can describe two things with the singular “one”; he cites the pearls and coral verse, although they come only from the salt sea. THALABI (عبد الرحمن بن زيد بن أسلم): They kneaded manna and quail together, making one food that they ate. WAHIDI-BASIT (ابن زيد): Ibn Zayd says manna was their food and quail their drink, but the two were combined when eaten and therefore counted as one food. BAGHAWI-FULL: Although manna and quail are two foods, Arabs may refer to two as one and one as two; the pearl-and-coral verse is an example, though only the salt sea produces them. BAGHAWI-FULL (عبد الرحمن بن زيد بن أسلم): ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam says they kneaded manna with quail, making one food. KASHSHAF-FULL: The single food means manna and quails, called one because they did not vary; even a varied dailymenu could be called one food if unchanged. IBNATIYYA-FULL: Ibn Atiyya says all of these grounds together establish the superiority of manna and quail. IBNATIYYA-FULL (الزجاج): Al-Zajjaj says manna and quail are superior in value, since the requested vegetables have little worth. IBNATIYYA-FULL: The Israelites spoke in the wilderness after tiring of manna and quail and recalling their former life in Egypt; the two foods are called one food because they ate them together and repeatedly received the same pair. TABRISI: They say they cannot endure one food: manna and quails are called one because the same daily food repeated from day to day, even if it offered varieties. TABRISI: A further interpretation contrasts farmed and crafted food with manna and quails given freely. IBNJAWZI-ZAD: The Israelites said this while in the wilderness; by one food they meant manna and quail. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (محمد بن القاسم): They counted manna and quail as one food because the manna was eaten with quail and the quail with manna. QURTUBI-FULL: Fifth, manna and quail were certainly lawful as gifts from God, whereas dealings in crops could involve usurpation and doubt. QURTUBI-FULL: They called manna and quail one food though they were two because they ate one together with the other. QURTUBI-FULL (قيل): Another view says the two foods repeated daily, so they were called one regular fare, like a person constant in one practice. BAYDAWI-FULL: The single food they could no longer bear was manna and quails from the wilderness. NASAFI-FULL: The one food was manna and quail; it was called one because it did not change, as a person may call a daily unchanging menu one food despite its variety. NASAFI-FULL: Alternatively, they considered manna and quail one kind because both were refined foods, while they wanted the vegetables and grains familiar to an agricultural people. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (ابن زيد): Ibn Zayd says the Israelites mixed manna and quail, making them like one color that combines several things. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (قيل): Some take the one food to mean quail, since manna was a drink or sweet accompaniment and only quail counted as food to them. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (قيل): Others compare calling two foods one to calling one source two, as in the verse about pearl and coral coming from two seas although they come only from the salty sea. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (قيل): Another view says they spoke while only one of the two foods was being sent down. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (الزمخشري): Al-Zamakhsharī explains one food as the unchanged manna and quail, which they called one because it did not vary from day to day. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (الزمخشري): Another explanation is that manna and quail were one class of luxurious fare, while the Israelites as agricultural people wanted familiar varied crops and vegetables. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (الزجاج): The first explanation measures superiority by value: vegetables are of little worth beside the more valuable manna and quails. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (قيل): A second explanation says manna and quails were God's gift and commanded food, so continuing to obey and thank Him earned reward in the afterlife, unlike the requested food. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (قيل): A fourth explanation values freedom from toil: manna and quails came without labor, while crops required cultivation and care. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (قيل): A fifth explanation values lawful purity: manna and quails came from God free of the defects, usurpation, unlawful elements, and doubts that can affect crops. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (قيل): A sixth explanation says manna and quails are superior in the kind of nourishment and benefit they provide. ABUHAYYAN-FULL: The request refers to the vegetables and grains they chose over manna and quails. SAMIN-DURR: Although manna and quails are two foods, واحد can mean one unchanging, nonvarying kind. n": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:61/q08/p1", "position": "Food or nourishment, including what is eaten or drunk", "reasons": "NAHHAS: يا موسى is a singular vocative; لن makes نصبر subjunctive, على makes طعام genitive, and واحد is its adjective. JISHUMI: Ṭaʿām means food or nourishment; ṭaʿm with ḍamma means eating, ṭaʿm also means taste, and food can denote nourishing substance. TABRISI: Ṭabrisī defines food as nourishment, ṭaʿm as eating, and food also as a physical substance perceived by taste. QURTUBI-FULL: An unnamed poet describes ostriches at Wajrah as tasting sleep only while fasting, illustrating the idiom. QURTUBI-FULL (أبو خراش): Abū Khirāsh's poetry uses ṭaʿm first for food and then for its savor or desirability. QURTUBI-FULL: Ṭaʿām can mean anything eaten or drunk; Qur'anic 'taste' can include drinking wine, and honey as salwā would also be a drink. QURTUBI-FULL: Food can conventionally mean grain or dates specifically; Abū Saʿīd's report on zakāt al-fiṭr contrasts a measure of food with barley. QURTUBI-FULL: With fatḥah, ṭaʿm can mean what taste conveys or something desirable; with ḍammah it means food. ABUHAYYAN-FULL: Ṭaʿām means whatever is eaten, analogously to ʿaṭāʾ for whatever is given, and is a generic noun. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (قيل): One explanation follows the singular grammatical form of ṭaʿām, not the fact that it refers to two foods. SAMIN-DURR: لن نصبر على طعام واحد is a subject–predicate clause, and the whole clause is an object of the verb of saying. SAMIN-DURR: The phrase ما يطعم النوم means does not sleep; a poem uses it for ostriches that sleep only standing. SAMIN-DURR: طعام can mean anything eaten or drunk, as in 2:249, but sometimes refers specifically to certain foods such as grain or dates; a charity hadith distinguishes a measure of food from barley. SAMIN-DURR: طعم can also mean giving; the prophetic report إذا استطعمكم الإمام فأطعموه means prompt the imam when he asks for a cue."}]}
{"id": "2:61/q09", "question": "How is فَٱدْعُ pronounced and parsed?", "turns_on": "The usual imperative vowel versus the Banū ʿĀmir dialect and its grammatical explanation.", "positions": [{"id": "2:61/q09/p1", "position": "Kasra in the Banū ʿĀmir form", "reasons": "NAHHAS: فادع is a request functioning like an imperative, so its wāw is dropped; Banū ʿĀmir pronounce its ʿayn with kasra at the consonant junction. QURTUBI-FULL: Banū ʿĀmir pronounce fa-dʿu with kasrah on ʿayn at the consonant meeting, treating the defective verb like a sound verb. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (بنو عامر): The Banū ʿĀmir dialect pronounces the command fa-dʿi with kasra on the ʿayn, treating daʿā as a weak verb like ramā-yarmī."}, {"id": "2:61/q09/p2", "position": "The imperative has a dialectal form", "reasons": "ZAJJAJ: He prefers construing the following verb as the response to an imperative, as with “tell My servants to establish prayer”; Qur’anic imperatives without a jussive particle are otherwise indicative. {"id": "2:61/q10", "question": "What are they asking Moses to do?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:61/q10/p1", "position": "They ask Moses to petition God for them", "reasons": "THALABI: Fa-dʿu means “ask,” and lanā means “for us.” WAHIDI-BASIT (قتادة): Qatada says they remembered their former Egyptian food and asked Moses to pray for it; ta'am is a generic term for what is eaten. WAHIDI-BASIT (أصحاب المعاني): Some linguists say food was called one because their daily nourishment never changed, like someone described as following one regular course by keeping to fasting and prayer. WAHIDI-BASIT: The petition is expressed in the past tense as an optimistic expression that it has already happened. BAGHAWI-FULL: “Ask for us” means ask God on our behalf. BAYDAWI-FULL: They ask Moses to petition his Lord on their behalf. ABUHAYYAN-FULL: The Israelites were weary of the wilderness and repetitive food, distant from their familiar land and habits; they expressed impatience and asked Moses to petition God for them. ABUHAYYAN-FULL: The second ذلك may repeat the earlier reference to punishment, or point to disbelief and killing; on the latter reading it is neither repetition nor emphasis. BURSEVI: The request asks Moses to supplicate for them; the connective “so” makes their inability to endure the diet the cause of the request. ALUSI-FULL: The phrase asks Moses to pray on their behalf for the listed produce; the conjunction marks their impatience as the reason for asking. ALUSI-FULL (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): The Prophet asked ʿUmar to include him among those for whom he prayed. ALUSI-FULL (الأثر): A transmitted saying urges prayer through tongues that have not disobeyed God, understood here as other people's tongues. IBNASHUR-FULL: On either reading, both باءs are causal; Ibn ʿĀshūr rejects making one mean مع, since repetition can replace conjunction without the strained reading in al-Kashshāf and al-Ṭībī."}]}
{"id": "2:61/q11", "question": "What does the supplication word mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:61/q11/p1", "position": "Supplication is a humble request to one above", "reasons": "THALABI (أبو عبيدة): Abū ʿUbayda says the phrase means they bore and acknowledged it, comparing it to the prophetic supplication “I acknowledge Your favor upon me and my sin”; God’s anger means blame, threat, and punishment, and likewise hatred and wrath. TABRISI (ابن السراج): Ibn al-Sarraj derives duʿāʾ, supplication, from nidāʾ, calling. ABUHAYYAN-FULL: Duʿāʾ is calling aloud by the name of the person invoked, from daʿā/yadʿū. ABUHAYYAN-FULL: A Prophetic supplication uses باء for both a blessing and a sin, confirming the two usages. SAMIN-DURR: دعاء here means asking, but can also mean naming or calling, as in the quoted poem دعتني أخاها. BURSEVI: Bursevī cites al-Baghawī’s note that Arabic can use a dual form for one thing, as in the phrase about pearls and coral, which come only from salt water. ALUSI-FULL: The proposal that a singular “one” stands for two foods is still less plausible; the cited comparison uses a dual expression for pearls that come from only one sea. ALUSI-FULL: Calling God “Lord” prepares the grounds for the prayer's acceptance."}]}

{"id": "2:61/q13", "question": "How does يُخْرِجْ depend on the preceding request?", "turns_on": "Imperative response, an implied command, supplication, or omitted command lām.", "positions": [{"id": "2:61/q13/p1", "position": "The verb is jussive in the petition", "reasons": "AKHFASH: The added من is not confined to negation and questions: it appears in the cited verse and in ordinary expressions such as “Zayd is among the best.” AKHFASH: Common idioms omit an understood noun: “Do you want …?” means “Do you have a need for …?”, and “no harm on you” is similarly elliptical. SAMIN-DURR: When a damma before و creates a long vowel, that length blocks assimilation between identical following sounds, so the letters remain distinct, as in آمنوا وعملوا and الذي يوسوس. {"id": "2:61/q15", "question": "What does the first min in mimmā do?", "turns_on": "Partitive or extra min in an affirmative clause, with or without an omitted object.", "positions": [{"id": "2:61/q15/p1", "position": "Partitive min", "reasons": "AKHFASH: The first من is partitive: the earth produces some unspecified amount of its plants, with the word “something” left unexpressed. TAB-FULL: Al-Tabari reads min as partitive: the Israelites asked for some of what the earth produces, so the particle itself supplies the partitive sense. TABRISI: Min in mimmā is partitive because they sought some of what the earth produces, not everything; the alternative treats it as redundant, but min is added only in negation. IBNJAWZI-NUZHA: Min is a genitive preposition used for partitive meaning, beginning point, and explanation of a kind; context also licenses figurative uses.
